Surah al-Ghashiyah (The Overwhelming)

Makkan without any dispute, and its number of verses is twenty-six likewise.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it on Friday together with its companion surah, as al-Nu'man ibn Bashir reported and as Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah recorded.

Page 112

When Allah, glory be to Him, had earlier alluded in brief to the believer and the disbeliever, and to Paradise and Hell, He here set out the matter in detail, so He said, Mighty is His saying:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ It has been said that ﴿هل﴾ (hal) here means ﴿قد﴾ (qad, "indeed"), and this is the apparent meaning of the words of Qutrub, where he said: that is, "Indeed there has come to you, O Muhammad, the report of the Overwhelming." The preferred view, however, is that it is an interrogative, and it is an interrogative intended to express wonder at what it introduces, to create eagerness to hear it, and to signal that it is one of the marvellous reports which narrators ought to pass on to one another and which those who retain knowledge should compete to receive.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a woman who was reciting: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ So he stood, peace and blessings be upon him, listening, and said: 'Yes, indeed it has come to me.'"

"Al-Ghashiyah" means the Resurrection, as Sufyan and the majority have said, and it was so named because it overwhelms people with its hardships and encompasses them with its terrors. Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Jubayr said:

It is the Fire, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the Fire will overwhelm their faces﴾ and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and above them will be coverings of fire﴾. But this is not correct, for what is to be shown of its report is not restricted to the Fire and its people, rather it speaks also of the conditions of the people of Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 88, verses 2–3:**

﴿Wujuhun yawma'idhin﴾ (Faces, that Day). The word ﴿wujuhun﴾ is in the nominative case and is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence). It is permissible to begin a sentence with it even though it is indefinite (*nakirah*), because it occurs in a context of classification (*mawdi' al-tanwi'*). It has also been said that the sense of the sentence is "owners of faces" (*ashab wujuh*), the predicate (*khabar*) being what follows. The adverbial phrase ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is linked to that predicate, and the tanwin (nunation) on ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is a substitute (*'iwad*) for a clause that is implied by the context.

﴿al-ghashiyah﴾ (the Overwhelming), that is, on a Day when it (the Overwhelming) comes over them. The sentence from here up to the words of the Most High ﴿mabthuthah﴾ (scattered) is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) that comes as an answer to a question arising from the rhetorical interrogative of arousing interest (*al-istifham al-tashwiqi*). It is as if it were said on his behalf, peace be upon him: "Has the news of it not reached you? What is it?" Then it was said: ﴿Wujuhun﴾, and so on.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: The news of it had not yet reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so Allah, glorified is He, informed him about it, and the Exalted said: ﴿Wujuhun yawma'idhin khashi'ah﴾ (Faces, that Day, will be humbled). The meaning of *khashi'ah* is "abased" (*dhalilah*). It was not described with abasement from the outset, because the description with *khushu'* (humility) carries an allusion to mockery (*tahakkum*), namely that they did not humble themselves at a time when humility would benefit them.

The same applies to the description with work in the words of the Glorified: ﴿'amilah﴾ (laboring), according to what has been said. This and the words of the Most High ﴿nasibah﴾ (toiling) are two further predicates of ﴿wujuh﴾, since what is meant by it is its owners. There are other possibilities regarding this, which will come, Allah willing. That is: laboring in that Day, weary in it. This refers to the Fire, as has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Their labor in it, as has been said, is dragging the chains and the shackles, wading in it like camels in mud, and climbing up and down its hills and valleys. This is the recompense for their arrogance toward work and toward obedience to Allah in the world.

It is related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: ﴿'amilah﴾ means (laboring) in the world, ﴿nasibah﴾ (toiling) in it, because they were not upon guidance, so they had no fruit except toil, and its end is the Fire. This was also reported in another narration from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. The apparent meaning is that, according to these scholars, the humility remains as it is in the Hereafter. In that case, ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ has no connection in meaning to the two descriptions, rather their connection is in the world. The weakness of this view is not hidden, and it is evident that work does not occur in the Hereafter; even if this is granted, it does not remove its remoteness.

'Ikrimah said: ﴿'amilah﴾ (laboring) refers to the world, and ﴿nasibah﴾ (toiling) refers to the Day of Resurrection. The apparent meaning is that the humility is as already mentioned. There is no hiding the remoteness of making the enclosed (*al-muhat*) by two temporal references a past-tense (*madi*) expression.

It has been said that the three descriptions all refer to the world, and the speech follows the pattern of the verse:

*"Idha ma intasabna lam taladni la'imah"*
(When we trace lineage, no base woman bore me);

that is, it becomes evident to them on that Day that she (the face) was humble, laboring and toiling in the world for no benefit. Before that Day, they used to think that they were doing good works. These are the ascetics (*nussak*) of the Jews and the Christians, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and it includes others resembling them among the ascetics of the people of error. This view is more remote than its two companions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 88, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Burning in a scorching fire﴾, meaning intensely hot, from "hamiyat al-nar" (the fire became hot) when its heat intensified, is another predicate (khabar) for ﴿faces﴾. All of these, as you see, [are weak]. It is also permitted that this and what follows it, of the two clauses, be a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the details of their conditions. Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin, read: "'amilatun nasibah" with the accusative (nasb), by way of censure (dhamm). Abu Raja', Ibn Muhaysin, Ya'qub, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "tusla" with a dammah on the taa', and Kharijah read "tusalla" with a dammah on the taa', a fatha on the sad, and a shaddah on the lam, for emphasis (mubalaghah).

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾ (āniyah), meaning it has reached its utmost heat, so it is at its most intense in heat, as in His words, ﴿between it and a fiercely boiling water﴾ (ḥamīm āns). This is the well-known interpretation. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid. Ibn Zayd said: it means "present/ready for them," from their saying anā al-shayʾ, "the thing was present." But this is not correct.

﴿They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ﴾. This clarifies their food after clarifying their drink. Ḍarīʿ, as ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, is dry shibraq (a kind of plant). According to ʿIkrimah, it is a thorny tree lying flat on the ground. Others said: it is a kind of thorny plant which camels graze when it is fresh, but when it dries they avoid it, and it is a deadly poison. Abū Dhu'ayb said:

*He grazed on the lush shibriq until it withered and became ḍarīʿ, and the nahāʾis departed from him.*

Ibn Gharārah al-Hudhalī said, describing camels and poor pasture:

*They were confined in the hazm of ḍarīʿ, so all of them are hunch-backed, bleeding in both hands, and unruly.*

Some lexicographers said: ḍarīʿ is the dried ʿarfaj when it is broken. Al-Zajjāj said: it is a plant like the ʿawsaj (a thorny shrub). Al-Khalīl said: it is a green plant with a foul smell which the sea casts up. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is ḍarīʿ in its literal sense. It was also said: it is a fiery tree resembling ḍarīʿ. You know that He who brought fire out of the green tree (cf. Q. 36:80) is not incapable of making ḍarīʿ grow in the fire. Yes, what supports what was said is what al-Baghawī narrated, via Ibn ʿAbbas, raising it (to the Prophet ﷺ): "Ḍarīʿ is a thing in the Fire, similar to thorns, more bitter than aloes, more foul-smelling than a carcass, and hotter than fire."

If this is authentic, then so be it. Ibn Kaysān said: it is a food over which they humble themselves, abase themselves and beseech God for deliverance from it, and so it was named thus. Accordingly, it may be a tree or something else. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan and a group that it is al-zaqqūm. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr that it is stones in the Fire. It was also said: it is a valley in Hell, meaning they have no food except from that place. Perhaps it is the place into which the pus of the people of the Fire flows, which is ghislīn. On this basis the reconciliation is between this restriction and the restriction in His words, ﴿nor any food except from ghislīn﴾, apparently, in that their food from that valley is the ghislīn which flows into it. Likewise if what Ibn Kaysān said is intended, and it is one with it. Zaqqūm may also be one with both of them on this basis. Its identity with ḍarīʿ, on the view that it is a tree, is close.

It was said in reconciliation: ḍarīʿ is a metaphor or a kināyah (allusion), and what is meant is a hateful food, even for camels and other animals that enjoy grazing thorns. So it does not contradict its being zaqqūm or ghislīn. It was also said: what is intended is that they have no food at all, because ḍarīʿ is not food even for beasts, let alone people, as one says: "So-and-so has no shade except the sun," meaning he has no shade. On this is understood His words, ﴿nor any food except from ghislīn﴾, and His words, ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqūm, the food of the sinner﴾ (Q. 44:43–44), so there is no contradiction at all.

It was said: ghislīn, which is pus, is by divine power such that He makes it in the form of ḍarīʿ and zaqqūm, so their food is ghislīn and zaqqūm, which are ḍarīʿ. Its strain is not hidden from the one who is suckling (i.e., a child). It may also be said, in reconciliation, on the view that the three are distinct in essence: torment has varieties, and the tormented are of levels. Among them are those who eat zaqqūm, among them those who eat ghislīn, and among them those who eat ḍarīʿ; each gate has its allotted portion.

﴿Neither nourishes nor relieves from hunger.﴾ It may be in a position of genitive (jarr) as a qualifier (ṣifah) of *ḍarī'* (a thorny plant, *ḍarī'*). The meaning is that their food is from a thing that is not among the foods of humans, but is thorns. Thorns are among what camels graze on and find delightful, and this is a kind of it from which they recoil and do not approach. The two benefits of nourishment are negated from it: the removal of hunger and the provision of strength and fatness in the body. If you wish, you may say: it is from a disliked thing, one humbles oneself before it, supplicates to God the Exalted, and asks Him, glorified is He, for deliverance from it, and it has none of the two benefits of nourishment at all. It may also be in a position of nominative (raf') as a qualifier of the implied *ṭa'ām* (food), since the sense is: "They have no food except food of *ḍarī'*." The meaning is close to what has been mentioned. It is not permissible for it to be a qualifier of the mentioned noun (*ḍarī'*), for then it would not indicate that their food is confined to *ḍarī'*; rather it would indicate that what does not nourish nor relieves hunger from their food is confined to it, and this spoils the meaning. As for it having no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), it is on the basis that it is a new, independent sentence (*mustaʾnaf*), and the first (view) is more apparent.

It is narrated that the disbelievers of Quraysh said, when they heard the first part of the verse: "Indeed, our camels grow fat upon *ḍarī'*!" So it was revealed: ﴿Neither nourishes﴾, and so on.

It is said: Then they either deny (this) or mock with it, and this is the more apparent, so their statement is refuted by the negation of fattening and satiety; or they affirm it, and the meaning then is that their food of *ḍarī'* is not of the kind of your *ḍarī'*; rather it is something that neither fattens nor relieves from hunger. According to the first (view), it is an emphasizing qualifier (ṣifah mu'akkidah), a rejection of what they claimed, not a clarifying qualifier (ṣifah kāshifah), since there is no obscurity; and according to the second, it is a restricting qualifier (ṣifah mukhaṣṣiṣah). In either case, the indefiniteness of *jū'* (hunger) is for belittlement, i.e., it does not relieve from any hunger whatsoever. The postponement of the negation of relief from hunger is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fawāṣil*) and as a means to explicitly negating both matters; for if it had been placed first, there would have been no need to mention the negation of fattening, because the negation of relief from hunger entails the negation of fattening. For this reason the negation (*lā*) was repeated, not for emphasis of negation. In *al-Irshad* (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, the tafsir of Abu al-Su'ud): The negation of both matters from it is not on the basis that they have a readiness for satiety and fattening, but that it does not produce either of them; rather it is on the basis that there is no readiness on their part and no benefit from it. The clarification of this is that their hunger and thirst are not of the kind known in this world, a condition arising in a human when nature calls for the replacement of what dissolves from the body, making him desire food and drink, so that he takes pleasure in them when eating and drinking, is content with them when they settle in the stomach, and gains strength and fatness from them when they are digested. Rather, their hunger is an expression of their compulsion, when the fire blazes in their bowels, to introduce something dense that fills it and expels what is in it of flame. Or, (it could be that) they have a longing for some food, and delight in it when eating, and are content with it without others, and gain strength; but far is that. Likewise, their thirst is an expression of their compulsion, when eating the *ḍarī'* and its burning in their bellies, to something liquid and cold to extinguish it, without their having any pleasure in drinking it or gaining any strength from it at all. This is the meaning of what is narrated: that God, may He be exalted, imposes hunger upon them to the point that they are compelled to eat *ḍarī'*; then when they eat it, thirst is imposed upon them, so they are compelled to drink *ḥamīm* (boiling water), which scorches their faces and cuts their intestines. May God the Exalted protect us and all Muslims from that. End of quotation.

This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and such a thing is not said on the basis of opinion (*ra'y*), and there is no basis in what we have reviewed for interpreting the apparent meanings for its sake. Thus the truth is that they have hunger, thirst, and desire for food and drink, just as the hungry and thirsty in this world have a desire for them; but for them there, these have reached their extreme, through God the Exalted, mighty and majestic, imposing them without an ordinary cause in the manner of this world. So they are compelled by it to *ḍarī'* and *ḥamīm*, just as one who is overcome by extreme hunger and thirst in this world is compelled to consume the disgusting, loathsome food and drink. But they gain no benefit from what they consume; rather they are increased in punishment upon punishment. We ask God the Exalted for pardon and well-being by His grace and generosity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 88, verses 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾ marks the beginning of relating the account of the people of Paradise, and the account of the people of the Fire is placed first because it is more effective in conveying the awe of the Overwhelming Event (al-Ghashiyah) and magnifying its report; and because relating the good condition of the people of Paradise after relating the evil condition of the people of the Fire adds to what is related both goodness and radiance. The discussion of its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is similar to what preceded. This sentence was not conjoined to that previous sentence only to signal the complete contrast between their two meanings. The word al-na'imah (joyful) may be derived from al-nu'mah (softness), and it is used as a metaphor for radiance and beauty of appearance, meaning: faces on that Day possessing radiance and beauty, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾. Or it may be derived from al-ni'mah (bliss), meaning: faces on that Day made to enjoy blessings. ﴿Content with their striving﴾, meaning: content with their deed which they performed in the worldly abode. It is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿content﴾, and the fronting of the phrase is for emphasis while observing the rhyme (fasilah). The lam here is not for causation; rather it is like the lam in "radiya bi-kadha" (he was pleased with such-and-such), so it is as if it were said: content with their striving. Some verifying scholars have mentioned that it serves to strengthen the verb's transitivity by itself, and therefore Sufyan said regarding this, as transmitted from him by Ibn Abi Hatim:

"They were pleased with their deed, and their being pleased with it is a metaphor or figure of speech for the fact that it has a praiseworthy outcome and that they are rewarded for it with the greatest and finest reward."

It has been permitted that the lam is for causation, meaning: content because of their striving in obedience to Allah, exalted is He, in that they were given what they were given of good. But this is not the correct view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 88, verses 10–11:

﴿In a lofty garden﴾ — elevated in place, or lofty in rank. Loftiness is either sensory (physical) or figurative (ma'nawi), and Abu Hayyan combined the two.

﴿Thou shalt not hear﴾ — an address to everyone who is fit to be addressed, or it is attributed to the feminine third-person pronoun, which refers to "faces" in the sense that their owners are meant. Alternatively, the attribution is metaphorical (majaz), and the same applies to what precedes it. Some have pointed out that the verse contains the rhetorical device of al-istikhdam (lit. "employment," a figure where a word is used in one sense and a pronoun referring back to it in another), by choice, since the word "faces" is first meant literally and, when the pronoun returns to it, it refers to their owners; they are the ones who do not hear.

﴿therein any idle talk﴾ — i.e., vain speech (laghw). It is a verbal noun (masdar) with the same meaning. It may also be an adjective of an omitted noun (kalima), in the sense of relative (lil-nisba): i.e., "a word possessing idle talk." It is permissible, on the assumption that it is an adjective, for the attribution to be metaphorical, because the word is what is subjected to idle talk, not the one engaging in it. It is also permissible that it be an adjective of an omitted self (nafs); i.e., "thou shalt not hear therein any soul engaging in idle talk," and it may be treated as heard because it is described by what is heard, as you say: "I heard Zayd saying such-and-such." It is also permissible that this be a metaphorical attribution as well.

Al-A'raj, the people of Makkah and Madinah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr (with a variant transmitted from them) recited: "lā tusma'u" with a feminine ta' and in the passive voice, "lāghiyatun" with a nominative ending. Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr likewise, except that they recited with the yā' (the third-person masculine prefix), because the feminine is metaphorical while a separating element is present. Al-Jahdari likewise, except that he put "lāghiyatan" in the accusative, on the meaning of "lā yusma'u fīhā aḥadun lāghiyatan" ("no one hears therein any idle talk"), from your saying: "asma'tu Zaydan" (I made Zayd hear).

*Istinaf* (a resumptive clause) that is brought to confirm what was detailed about the narration of the Overwhelming (*al-Ghashiyah*) and what is built upon it, namely the Resurrection about which they dispute, by citing as proof something they cannot deny. Abd ibn Humayd and others related from Qatadah that he said: "When God, exalted is He, described what is in Paradise, the people of misguidance marveled at that, so God, glorified and exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ and so on." This, in the Hereafter, comes down to denying the Resurrection, as is evident. The hamzah is for denial and reproach, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an omitted premise required by the context.

The word *kayfa* ("how") is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) referring to the subject of *khuliqat* ("was created"), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God?﴾. It is suspended from the verb of seeing (*mu'allaqah*), and the clause is an inclusive apposition (*badal ishtimal*) from *al-Ibil* ("the camels"). A clause may be an apposition for a preceding noun when it contains an interrogative, as in their saying: "I knew Zayd, who is he?" (*'araftu Zaydan abu man huwa*), according to the most correct opinions, since the Arabs have introduced *ila* ("to") directly before *kayfa* without an intervening apposition, just as they introduced it before *'ala*. Thus it is related from them that they said: "Look at how he does it" (*unzur ila kayfa yasna'*). And it is related from them that they said: "On what terms will you sell the two reds?" (*'ala kayfa tabi' al-ahmarayn*). Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr* and *al-Tadhkirah* and other works, mentioned that when the verb is suspended from what contains the interrogative, the interrogative does not remain in its true sense.

It has also been said that *kayfa* is an apposition from *al-Ibil*, but in *al-Mughni* this was criticized with what is open to question in part of it. In *Majma' al-Bayan* it was permitted for it to be in the position of an accusative as an adverbial (*al-masdar*), and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

The word *al-Ibil* applies to the many camel droppings (*al-bu'ran*), has no singular from its own form, and is feminine. For this reason, when it is diminutived, the *ta'* is added to it, so they say *ubaylah*. In the plural they say *a'bal*. They have also derived words from its form, so they say *abila* and *ta'abbala al-rajul* ("the man became camel-like/ enriched in camels"), and they expressed wonder at this verb irregularly, saying *ma a'bala Zaydan* ("how camel-rich Zayd is!"). According to what is reported, Sibawayh did not preserve a noun of the pattern *fi'il* with a kasra on both the *fa'* and the *'ayn* other than *ābil*.

*Ghayr ābil*, that is: do they deny what was indicated of the Resurrection and its rulings, and do they consider its occurrence far-fetched from the power of God, mighty and majestic is He? Then let them look at the camels, which are before their eyes, which they use at all times, how they were created: created in a wondrous manner, deviating from the customary patterns of the creation of most kinds of animals, in the greatness of their bodies, the strength of their power, and the marvelous and fitting shapes, by which they are able to perform the arduous tasks that proceed from them, such as rising with heavy loads while they are kneeling, and carrying crushing burdens to distant regions. They also endure hunger and thirst, to the extent that their thirst may reach *al-'ishr* (with a kasra then a sukun), which is eight days between two watering times, and it may be that this is possible; in that case they are called *al-hawazi*, with an unpointed *ha'* and a *zay*. They are satisfied with walking and grazing on whatever is available of thorns, trees, and other things that most other beasts can hardly graze. They also submit to people in movement and rest, in kneeling and rising, where people use them for these purposes as they wish, and every young and old person leads them by their halter. They are also affected by a beautiful voice despite the hardness of their livers, and so on. They were singled out for mention because they are the most wondrous animals among the Arabs, being the most noble of mounts and the most elaborately made, and the Arabs have the most complete knowledge of their conditions.

It is related from al-Hasan that they were singled out for mention because they eat date-pits and fodder (*al-qatt*) and produce milk. It was said to him: "The elephant is greater in wonder," and he said: "The Arabs are far removed from knowledge of the elephant. Moreover, it is a pig, whose meat is not eaten and whose back is not ridden," meaning: in the manner that the back of a camel is ridden without hardship in taming it, and its milk is not milked.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad said: "*Al-Ibil* here means the clouds, because the Arabs call them by this name, since they come in herds like camels and are driven as camels are driven, and in their forms they sometimes resemble camels." That is, he intends them here in the manner of metaphor and figurative speech. It seems, as al-Zamakhshari said, that the one who said this only sought to achieve suitability among the things joined by coordination, according to what the rules of eloquence require, and this suitability is present even with the camels remaining in their pens. The Imam (al-Razi) said: "The suitability in it is that the address is to the Arabs, who are people of journeys on camels in the wastelands. Sometimes they travel alone on them, and the one who travels alone reflects, for lack of a companion to converse with and a distraction to occupy him, so he contemplates what his gaze falls upon. When he looks at what is with him, he sees the camel; when he looks upward, he sees the sky; when he looks right and left, he sees the mountains; and when he looks downward, he sees the earth. So he is commanded to look, in his solitude, at what these matters relate to his gaze, and thus there is a suitability between them on this basis."

Isam al-Din said: "The imagination of the Arabs combines these four, because their most precious property is camels, the source of water for them is the sky, their pasture is on the earth, and the protection of their property is by the mountains. Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 88, verse 25:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return (iyabahum)﴾ is a reason (ta'līl) for His, Exalted is He, punishing them with the greatest punishment. Iyab is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of āba, meaning "returned," i.e., indeed to Us is their return by death and resurrection, not to anyone other than Us, neither independently nor in partnership. The pronoun in it and in what follows is plural in consideration of the meaning of "man" (man), just as its singular form in what preceded is in consideration of its wording. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "iyyabahum" with a shadda on the yā'. Al-Baṭalyūsī said in his book al-Muthallathāt: This reading admits of two interpretations. One of them is that "iyyāb" with the shadda is fa''āl (fi'āl) from awiba, on the pattern of fa'ila, like kadhiba, kidhdhāban. Its origin is awwāb, and the first wāw was not considered a barrier because it was weak through being sukūn, so the second wāw was changed into a yā' because the hamza was kasra, becoming in estimation uwyābā, then the first was also changed into a yā' because of the gathering of a yā' and a wāw and the sukūn of one of them; and because if the first wāw does not prevent the second from changing, it is more worthy of changing. The second is that it is fayyāl, its origin being iywāb, treated like sayyid. Its verb in this case is ayyaba, on the pattern of fayyala, like ḥawqala, ḥaygalān, from al-iyāb, and its origin is iyawwub, which was treated as mentioned. The first aspect is more analogical, because they said in its verbal noun: al-ta'wīb, and the taf'īl is the verbal noun of fa'ala, not fay'al; and despite that they said: he is quick in awba and ayba; so it seems they preferred the yā' for its lightness. End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari also mentioned these two aspects, except that in the first of them he allows that its origin is awwāb, fa''āl, from awaba, then it was said iywāb like diwān in dawwān, then what was done to the origin of sayyid was done to it. Its apparent meaning is that the first wāw is the one changed first into a yā'. It is objected that it is established that if the first wāw is set for idghām and what precedes it is kasra, it is not changed into a yā' because of the kasra, as in ikhriwwāṭ, the verbal noun of ikhrawwaṭa; and that diwān, if it is mentioned for analogy with it and not as a comparison, is not suitable for that because of their explicit statement about its irregularity; and it seems al-Baṭalyūsī turned to what he turned to for this reason. In al-Kashf: If the verbal noun of fā'ala from al-awb is made, then fay'āl has come in it, to the extent that some said that fa''āl is lightened from it, it would be more apparent, because fay'al is not established except by a firm report, while the first is like the analogical; and the meaning of the doer then is either exaggeration or the mutual racing of some of them with others in returning. As for making it fa''āl according to what al-Zamakhshari established, it is farther, to the end of his words. Its being from fā'il was also permitted by Ibn 'Atiyya, but he said: It may be from āwib, so it comes as iywāb, its hamza made easy, and the necessary thing in idghām would return it to awwāb, but the yā' was preferred in it against analogy. Abu Hayyan objected to him that the saying of his: "and the necessary thing was etc." is not correct; rather the necessary thing, when idghām is considered, is that it should be iyyāb, because a yā', which is the one changed from the hamza by easing, and a wāw, which is the root letter of the word, have gathered, and one of them is quiescent, so the wāw is changed into a yā' and the yā' is assimilated into it, becoming iyyāb. So do not be heedless.

﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾, on the Gathering-place, not upon anyone else. The "then" (thumma) here denotes the **tarakhi rutbi** (a sequence of rank, i.e. a gradation in dignity, as opposed to sequence in time), not the temporal sequence. For the temporal sequence is between their return and their reckoning, not between the fact that their return is to Him, exalted is He, and the fact that their reckoning is upon Him, glorified is He, for these are two matters that are continuous. In beginning the two clauses with **inna** (indeed), placing its predicate first, using the pronoun of majesty, and conjoining the second to the first with **thumma**, which indicates how far the status of reckoning exceeds in severity the announcement of the utmost wrath that necessitates severe punishment, there is what is not hidden. And in the verse there is a refutation of many of the **Shi'ah**, who claimed that the reckoning of all creatures is upon the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, and they cited as evidence for that the reports that they fabricated against him and against the Household of his house, may Allah be pleased with them all. As for the meaning of his saying, may Allah ennoble his face: "I am the divider of Paradise and Hellfire" (if it is authentically established) that the people of this nation are of two groups: a group with me, who are upon guidance, and a group against me, who are upon error; so a portion is with me in Paradise and a portion in Hellfire, perhaps they meant that Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, reckons the creatures by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, just as others say that the angels, upon them be peace, reckon them by the command of the Majestic and Exalted. This is a meaning that does not contradict the restriction that the verse requires, but it has not been established. And what particularity is there in the Commander, may Allah ennoble his face, among all the prophets, messengers and the near-brought angels, upon them all be the prayers and peace, that would require it? There is no deficiency for him, may Allah ennoble his face, in negating that from him. And it suffices him, may Allah be pleased with him, of the manifestation of his honour on the Day of Resurrection that he will be escorted into Paradise between the Prophet and Ibrahim, upon them both and upon him be blessings and peace, as has come in the hadith, along with other things that will become apparent on that Day. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.
